title: Best gravel race bikes 2026 reviewed
content:
Cyclist
Best gravel race bikes 2026 reviewed

The design of the best gravel race bikes has changed drastically over the last couple of years. Whereas the first generation of gravel race bikes had features more like endurance road bikes, including narrowish tyre clearance, newer gravel race bikes have gone much wider, reflecting the needs of riders who may be spending eight hours or more in the saddle.

The newer gravel race bikes have often retained their predecessors’ aero features though, as speeds in gravel races have increased such that aerodynamics is a significant influence on rider times. In 2018, the winning average speed for Unbound 200 was 30.9 kmh / 19.2 mph; by 2025 it had increased to 37.8 kmh / 23.5 mph.

Often, bike makers will have both a gravel race bike and a gravel adventure bike in their range, such as the Specialized Crux and Diverge and the Trek Checkmate and Checkpoint. Trek has the even more adventure focused CheckOut for those in search of a full-suspension gravel bike and suspension forks are creeping into gravel races too, at least for longer distances.

Our guide to the best gravel bikes covers race, adventure and general options and you can read our guide to the best gravel adventure bikes if you’re more into exploring. But read on for our picks of the best gravel race bikes and a buyer’s guide to what to look for if you’re looking for a fast gravel bike for racing and on/off tarmac use.

Why trust Cyclist‘s advice

At Cyclist, we hand pick the best drop bar bikes to review for Cyclist magazine and our online review pages, and our readers are treated to in-depth coverage of all that’s new in the world of road and gravel riding. That means that we’ve ridden and reviewed the cream of the gravel race bikes available, know the features to look for in a gravel race bike and can pinpoint the pros and cons of each.

Bikes for review are selected by our team and we’re not paid for our reviews, so you can trust us to offer impartial advice and an unbiased opinion.

The best gravel race bikes reviewed

3T RaceMax2 Italia

£8,763 as tested | Buy here

  • Aero frame with 51mm tyre clearance
  • Superb handling and two-piece cockpit
  • Prices:
    • Racemax2 Italia X Red XPLR AXS PM/Torno/Super Record X: £14,119
    • Racemax2 Italia X Force XPLR AXS: £8,459Racemax2 Italia Record X: £6,683
    • Racemax2 Italia Force XPLR AXS: £6,598
    • Racemax2 Italia Rival XPLR AXS: £5,837
    • Racemax2 Italia X frameset: £5,331
    • Racemax2 Italia frameset: £4,061

The Italia at the end of its name indicates that the Racemax2 frame is made in Italy – there’s also a lower priced WPNT option that’s painted in Italy and the premium Italia X. It will accept tyres up to 51mm, but still keeps the chainstays down to 420mm and is designed to be aero, with a wide down tube to shield the bottles and a nose to the head tube to smooth the airflow over the wide headset bearings.

3T has tweaked the geometry to keep a racy ride feel despite the clearance. Handling on technical and flowy off-road is superb and acceleration is sharp, while the Racemax2 is pacy on less demanding surfaces. It’s a well thought-out bike that’s great fun to ride.

  • Read our full 3T Racemax2 Italia review

Argon 18 Anti Matter 

£7,495 as tested | Buy here

  • Fast, agile ride even on technical terrain
  • Prioritises speed over big hit compliance
  • Prices:
    • Anti Matter Red XPLR AXS: £10,495
    • Anti Matter Force XPLR AXS: £7,495
    • Anti Matter Rival XPLR AXS: £5,495
    • Anti Matter frameset: £4,395

Geared to the fast pace of modern gravel races, the Argon 18 Anti Matter boasts wind tunnel honed aero tube profiles and 55mm tyre clearance. The ride position is the same as the Nitrogen Pro aero road bike, developed and tested alongside it, although the Anti Matter’s geometry is a little slacker.

The bike is one of the fastest we’ve ridden on MTB trails and nimble too. The flip side of the racy ride is a tendency to transmit larger hits to the rider, although trail chatter is handled well. Argon points to the Dark Matter if you’re after greater compliance, while the Anti Matter prioritises speed and is 14.5 watts faster in its testing.

  • Read our full Argon 18 Anti Matter review

Argonaut Supernaut GR3

Approx £10,300 as tested | Buy here

  • High-end frame in standard sizes and builds
  • Fast-riding and stable once at speed
  • Prices:
    • Supernaut GR3 frameset: $6,500

Argonaut custom-builds most of its bikes in Bend, Oregon to fit the rider, but the Supernaut GR3 is built to a standard geometry and carbon layup chosen by the high-end brand. There’s a choice of frameset-only or a SRAM Red XPLR AXS build with Argonaut D33 wheels and upgrade options.

The Argonaut Supernaut’s geometry took some getting used to. With a 68.5° head tube, it’s so slack that there’s a tendency for wheel flop at lower speeds. Once you hit a fast descent the bike comes alive though, offering stability and allowing you to hold more speed than you’d usually dare. The chainstays are short, but still offer 50mm tyre clearance and, helped by the 7.8kg bike weight for the XL size, lead to nimble climbing. It’s not aero-refined, but the Supernaut GR3 is rapid and flatters your skills when riding fast.

  • Read our full Argonaut Supernaut GR3 review

BMC Kaius 01

From £4,999 | Buy here

  • Second generation bike has wider clearance and is more aero
  • Full range of mounting points, but no in-frame storage
  • Prices:
    • Kaius 01 One: £9,999
    • Kaius 01 Two: £7,299
    • Kaius 01 Three: £4,999
    • Kaius 01 frameset: £3,999

The first generation BMC Kaius borrowed much of its design from the Teammachine road bike, including the aero tube profiles and bottle cages. The top spec bike we reviewed weighed just 7.7kg and the Kauis was ridden to victory in the inaugural UCI Gravel World Championship by Pauline Ferrand-Prévot in 2022.

BMC has now launched a second generation Kaius, which we’ve yet to review. Tyre clearance has increased from 44mm to 52mm, there’s a claimed 12% improvement in aerodynamics, 63g lower frame weight and a longer trail for added stability.

  • Read our full BMC Kaius (first generation) review, check out the latest issue of Cyclist magazine to read our review of the new model

Cannondale SuperX

£12,500 as tested | Buy here

  • Aggressive race focus, but with compliance at the saddle
  • 7.2kg weight in top spec and 48mm tyre clearance
  • Prices:
    • SuperX LAB71: £10,800
    • SuperX 1: £6,500
    • SuperX 3: £4,800
    • SuperX 4 AXS: £3,500
    • SuperX LAB71 frameset: £4,900

Cannondale has based the design for the SuperX gravel race bike on the SuperSix Evo, but tuned the aerodynamics for a more gravel-like 35km/h, increased tyre clearance to 48mm and thinned out the seat tube, top tube and seat stays to add compliance. Top specs get the same aero bar/stem combo as the SuperSix Evo and the frame geometry and fit are close to it too.

The handling is direct and the rear compliance works well to keep the ride comfortable, although the front end feels less accommodating on chattery surfaces. We swapped the stock 40mm Vittoria T50s to 47mm Terreno Dry tyres, which helped increase traction and front end comfort.

The top spec LAB71 bike we reviewed has a 900g claimed frame weight, although it’s an expensive option. Cannondale offers lower specs built on a standard carbon frameset too, but there’s not much depth to the range if you’re looking for something more affordable.

  • Read our full Cannondale SuperX LAB71 review

Canyon Grail

From £2,499 | Buy here

  • Now with 57mm tyre clearance and a variable width Pace cockpit
  • Aerodynamics tuned for 35kph and lightweight bag options
  • Prices:
    • Grail CFR AXS: £7,600
    • Grail CFR Di2: £6,200
    • Grail CF SLX 8 AXS: £4,799
    • Grail CF SLX 7 Di2: £3,899
    • Grail CF 7 AXS: £3,499
    • Grail CF 7: £2,499

In 2026, Canyon updated the Grail, launching an all-new third generation of its gravel race bike. There’s a tyre clearance upgrade to 57mm from 42mm, which follows the trend to ever-wider tyres in gravel races. As with the previous Grail, there’s a choice of CF, CF SLX and CFR frame grades, with the lightest build weighing a claimed 7.9kg.

Canyon has tuned the aerodynamics for a 35kph gravel race pace and says it’s faster with 55mm tyres than the old Grail was with 40m rubber. To accommodate the wide tyres, the Grail is now 1x only. It now uses a more flared variant of the variable width Pace cockpit that Canyon fits across its road bike range and there’s a new frame bag that weighs a claimed 100g, as well as a lightweight top tube bag.

  • Read our 2026 Canyon Grail launch story, stay tuned for our full review coming soon

Cervélo Áspero-5

£10,000 as tested | Buy here

  • Fast, aggressive aero gravel race bike, but with adjustable cockpit
  • 45mm tyre clearance and Vittoria Corsa Pro Control tyres proved limiting
  • Prices:
    • Áspero-5 Red AXS 1: £10.250
    • Áspero-5 GRX Di2 1: £8.250
    • Áspero-5 Force AXS 1: £7,500
    • Áspero-5 frameset: POA

The Áspero-5 borrows from the S5 road bike to improve aerodynamics by 37 watts over the previous generation. There’s in-frame storage and top tube mounts, but otherwise the bike is pared down for fast gravel racing. Even in size 58, the top spec Áspero-5 weighs 7.7kg. It’s aggressive, fitted with shorter cranks, but has a two-piece cockpit.

The 45mm tyre clearance is less than many newer gravel race bikes though and the 42mm Vittoria Corsa Pro Control tyres that come fitted to all specs are only suitable for finer, dry gravel.

Cervélo also sells the toned-down, lower priced standard Áspero, which we’ve reviewed as well.

  • Read our full Cervélo Áspero-5 review

Enve Mog

Approx £10,200 as tested | Buy here

  • Racy geometry, but still room for 50mm tyres
  • Fast, agile ride with the mounting points for bikepackers
  • Prices:
    • Mog Pro Red XPLR: $12,500
    • Mog Premium Red XPLR: $11,250
    • Mog Premium Force XPLR: $9,750
    • Mog Foundation Force XPLR: $8,250
    • Mog frameset: $4,100

Enve says it’s aimed for a balance between stability and capability with the Mog, but still considers it a gravel race bike. The aero profiled frame has 50mm clearance for 700c tyres, although the bike is aimed more at 44mm. The geometry favours a more racy ride feel and is akin to that of the Specialized Roubaix, while the spec tested, awash with Enve kit, weighed just 8.2kg.

The Mog’s combination of almost road bike speed on tarmac and agility on singletrack impressed, although we reckon it’s best suited to US style gravel racing. Despite this, Enve gives you a complete suite of mounting points, including fork leg bosses and down tube storage, so the Mog could do double-duty for bikepacking.

  • Read our full Enve Mog review

Factor Elara

From £5,899 (frameset) | Buy here

  • 57mm tyre clearance and 1x and 2x compatible
  • Aero optimised with wide stance fork
  • Prices:
    • Elara Red XPLR w/PM: £10,599
    • Elara Record X: £9,499
    • Elara Force XPLR w/PM: £8,999
    • Elara frameset: £5,899

The Elara is Factor’s replacement for the Ostro Gravel and shows how gravel race bike design has moved on, with tyre clearance increased to 57mm and an updated, longer geometry that is more road race bike than gravel. Despite compatibility with both 1x and 2x groupsets and chainrings with up to 52 teeth, the chainstays are short at 423mm.

In-frame storage helps keep your gear more aero, while the Elara’s wide stance fork design mirrors the One aero road bike and, Factor claims, helps offer aerodynamics comparable to a road race bike and 8% less than the Ostro Gravel. There are new 64mm deep Black Inc wheels with a 30mm internal width and 1,620g claimed weight.

The Elara joins the Factor Aluto and Sarana in the brand’s updated gravel bike portfolio, which is designed to cover the spectrum of modern gravel racing.

  • Read our Factor Elara launch story, review coming soon

Factor Sarana

From £8,299 as tested | Buy here

  • Large 57mm tyre clearance fits XC MTB tyres
  • Stable ride, with a suspension fork option
  • Prices:
    • Sarana Red XPLR w/PM: £9,399
    • Sarana Force XPLR w/PM: £7,699
    • Sarana frameset: £4,599

The Sarana targets ultra-distance gravel races, with a design that Factor says ensures stability and performance once the rider becomes fatigued after many hours in the saddle. That translates to a long wheelbase and stability, with 57mm tyre clearance, which is among the widest available in a gravel bike. The long front centre helps ensure stability on technical descents.

There’s the option to add a suspension fork or use a rigid fork and Factor includes bag mounts and in-frame storage for the needs of ultra riders and sells bags to match. Despite the stability and tyre clearance, the curved seat tube has allowed Factor to keep the chainstay length at 425mm, while increasing compliance. It’s a niche gravel race bike, but one which suits the trend to longer gravel races.

  • Read our full Factor Sarana review

FiftyOne Assassin

£2,499 (frameset) as tested | Buy here

  • Front and rear flip chips to tune the ride
  • Handling can be changed between edgy and precise or stable and relaxed
  • Prices:
    • Assassin SRAM Force: £4,299
    • Assassin GRX Di2 2X: £3,999
    • Assassin GRX Di2 1x: £3,899
    • Assassin SRAM Apex: £3,399
    • Assassin GRX 800: £3,399
    • Assassin GRX 600: £3,199
    • Assassin frameset: £2,499

The FiftyOne Assassin is made in Asia rather than the brand’s native Dublin. Tyre clearance is 47mm with both 1x and 2x drivetrains. It’s a fast gravel bike designed for double duties, with a full set of mounts and even dynamo cable routing. Front and rear flip-chips in the dropouts allow you to alter both the trail and the wheelbase, so you can swap between a more stable ride or snappier handling.

The effect on handling is dramatic, with a descent that’s relaxed in long setup feeling edgy when switched to short geometry, which is equally great for twisty singletrack and for road riding. The flip side of the flip chips is some extra weight – around 8.9kg – and lack of compatibility with SRAM XPLR groupsets.

  • Read our full FiftyOne Assassin review

Open Upper 2.0

£9,357 as tested | Buy here

  • Road bike geometry with 46mm tyre clearance
  • Fast and fun on road and off-road
  • Prices:
    • Upper 2.0 frameset: €5,300

Like the BMC Kaius, the Open Upper has undergone an epiphany, with the new version adding clearance. Although this is still only 46mm, Open reckons that’s enough for fast riders on road and light gravel. The Wide 2.0 has 66mm clearance if you want more.

The updated bike also has front-end integration, although with a design that allows 15mm of stem length adjustment. You can also choose an aero fork or one with mounts. The in-built compliance features soak up surface imperfections without slowing you down and Open has increased the frame’s front-centre to add stability. The 7.3kg weight is competitive too.

  • Read our full Open Upper 2.0 review

Orbea Terra Race

£9,899 as tested | Buy here

  • Pacy ride and great handling
  • Spec and colour customisation options
  • Prices:
    • Terra Race M12eLTD 1x PWR £8,799
    • Terra Race M11eLTD 1x PWR £8,799
    • Terra Race M21eLTD 1x £5,799
    • Terra Race M22LTD 1x £5,549
    • Terra Race M20iLTD £5,299
    • Terra Race M31eLTD 1x £4,799
    • Terra Race M20LTD £4,399
    • Terra Race OMX frameset £3,299

Built from Orbea’s premium OMX carbon fibre, the Terra Race frame is claimed to weigh 910g in size M, with the aero fork adding 425g. Official tyre clearance is 45mm, but gravel racers have fitted 50s. Orbea has tuned the frame’s aerodynamics and fitted an integrated cockpit and 50mm deep Oquo wheels. Compliance is assured by features such as a round seatpost and lowered stays, while in-frame storage has been removed to lower weight and the geometry is designed for stability at speed.

There are plenty of customisation choices, including 11 cockpit sizes, different crank lengths and wheelsets and custom paint. Despite its racy design, the Terra Race was at home and comfortable on English winter rides, with plenty of seatpost extension to soak up rough surfaces and the low weight making for nimble climbing.

  • Read our full Orbea Terra Race review

Ribble Ultra-Grit

£7,499 as tested | Buy here

  • Fast ride from reactive, low weight frame
  • Can be a little firm on rougher stretches, but option to spec a suspension fork
  • Prices:
    • Ultra-Grit Red XPLR AXS: £7,549
    • Ultra-Grit Force XPLR AXS: £4,449
    • Ultra-Grit Rival XPLR AXS: £3,149
    • Ultra-Grit Apex XPLR AXS: £2,649
    • Ultra-Grit Sportfit Apex XPLR AXS (flat bar): £2,649

Ribble designed the Ultra-Grit around the needs of its own gravel racing team, with 53mm front/50mm rear tyre clearance. It’s made from a mix of carbon that includes Mitsubishi M46J, with a sub-900g claimed frame weight. Aerodynamics are ported from the Ultra-Race road bike, with a narrow-to-wide down tube shape that includes storage and shields the water bottles, while Ribble still provides a full array of mounts, even for mudguards.

The Ultra-Grit is fast to accelerate thanks to the frame’s rigid spine, although this does transmit trail vibration on rougher surfaces. Ribble has designed the rear of the bike to help temper this somewhat, however. It’s a bike designed for speed, while there’s the option to spec a RockShox suspension fork via Ribble’s bike builder if more compliance is wanted.

  • Read our full Ribble Ultra-Grit review

Scott Addict Gravel

£5,399 as tested | Buy here

  • Fast handling but stable off-road
  • Better for tamer gravel and tarmac than technical riding
  • Prices:
    • Addict Gravel Premium: £7,999
    • Addict Gravel 10: £5,799
    • Addict Gravel 20: £4,999
    • Addict Gravel 30: £3,499
    • Addict Gravel 40: £2,499
    • Addict Gravel 10 frameset: £2,949
    • Addict Gravel 20 frameset: £1,949

The Scott Addict Gravel is another gravel bike that’s as at home on the road as off, with 45mm tyre clearance and an 8.9kg weight in the 10 spec reviewed. Trade up to the RC spec and you can drop that to around 8kg. The long frame and short stem offer off-road stability with sharp handling and keep the reach to the bars in check.

The Addict Gravel is a bike for easier, hardpacked gravel, but we found it less surefooted on singletrack or rougher surfaces. It’s stiff though, so it climbs and corners well and the aero frame profiles may offer some free speed. Despite the fast gravel leanings, you can still fit mudguards.

  • Read our full Scott Addict Gravel review

Specialized Crux

£11,999 as tested | Buy here

  • Weights from 7.1kg
  • Responsive, stiff and now with 55mm tyre clearance
  • Prices:
    • S-Works Crux 5 LTD: £12,999
    • S-Works Crux 5 Red XPLR: £11,999
    • Crux 5 S-Level: £8,749
    • Crux 5 Expert: £5,999
    • Crux 5 Comp: £3,999
    • Crux 5 Sport: £3,249
    • S-Works Crux 5 frameset: £5,249

£13,000 for a gravel bike! But Specialized claims that the second generation S-Works Crux weighs just 7.1kg. It’s more capable too, with 55mm tyre clearance and aero profiles borrowed from the Tarmac making it 15.2 watts more aero. It’s fitted with 1,340g aero gravel wheels and now has integrated cabling through the new one-piece gravel cockpit.

Specialized has also relaxed the geometry for better handling when it gets technical, with the new Crux proving its capabilities with 1-2s in both the men’s and women’s Unbound 200 races in 2026. It’s fast and stiff and promotes a low, aero ride position.

You don’t have to spend £12,000 on your next gravel bike though, with the range starting with the £4,000 Comp spec with an 8.9kg claimed weight. There’s also a new S-Level spec that’s made of less flashy carbon than the S-Works bike, but still has much of the same hardware bolted to it.

  • Read our Specialized S-Works Crux first ride review

Trek Checkmate SLR

From £7,000 as tested | Buy here

  • Lightweight, aero and stiff, tempered by 45mm tyre clearance
  • A great all-road option, not just a gravel race bike
  • Prices:
    • Checkmate SLR 9 AXS £8,950
    • Checkmate SLR 7 AXS £7,000
    • Checkmate SLR frameset £4,200

As with many brands, Trek has differentiated its current generation gravel bikes into the adventure focused and the gravel race, with the Checkmate’s high spec frame leading to a 7.63kg weight for our top spec size L review bike. The Checkmate is aero too, borrowing from the Madone Gen 8 and with a geometry that promotes a more tucked ride position. It also uses the same bar/stem combo as the Madone, although with the Domane’s Isospeed decoupler at the rear. Trek currently offers just two UK specs (four worldwide), as well as a frameset option.

We found the low weight, aerodynamics and stiffness made for a really fun ride both off-road and on, although it’s better suited to fast, dry trails than technical terrain. We reckon whatever the Domane can do, the Checkmate can do better, making it a serious contender not just for gravel racing but all-road riding too.

  • Read our full Trek Checkmate SLR 9 AXS review

Wilier Rave SLR ID2

From £4,150 as tested | Buy here

  • Aero design features shared with the Filante SRL ID2 road race bike
  • 52mm tyre clearance, although fitted tyres are better for light gravel than mud
  • Prices:
    • Rave SLR ID2 Super Record 13 w/ power meter €10,700
    • Rave SLR ID2 SRAM Red XPLR AXS w/ power meter €10,600
    • Rave SLR ID2 SRAM Red XPLR AXS w/o power meter €9,900
    • Rave SLR ID2 Force XPLR AXS w/ power meter €9,000
    • Rave SLR ID2 Force XPLR AXS w/o power meter €7,800
    • Rave SLR ID2 GRX Di2 €6,600
    • Rave SLR ID2 Rival XPLR AXS €6,100
    • Rave SLR ID2 GRX Di2/Rival XPLR AXS w/ Miche Graff wheels €4,900
    • Rave SLR ID2 frame kit €4,200

Wilier offers a range of drag-reducing features in the Rave SLR ID2, including aero tube profiles, a one-piece cockpit on higher specs and an hourglass head tube. There’s more than a passing resemblance to the Filante SLR ID2 pro-level road race bike.

The 52mm tyre clearance offers plenty of scope to swap in wider tyres and the 27mm internal width hookless Miche gravel wheels are designed to support these. The UDH hanger allows Wilier to spec AXS XPLR 13-speed groupsets. We rated the lively, balanced ride feel and fast ride, although the 45mm Schwalbe G-One Allround tyres are better suited to gravel roads than UK mud.

  • Read our full Wilier Rave SLR ID2 review

What should I look for in a gravel racing bike?

If you want to go fast on gravel, here’s what to look for.

Weight

Gravel race bikes prioritise low weight over extra comfort features. In this, they’re much like the best road race bikes, with bike brands often using the same carbon fibre grades in their premium gravel race bikes as in their road bikes. You can choose a spec with top tier components to shave weight too.

The Specialized Crux, above, is the extreme example, but many of the best gravel race bikes hover around 8kg, a weight that would grace a road bike.

The downside, of course, is high price, but usually there are multiple specs that offer more affordable options with a slightly higher weight but similar ride qualities.

Geometry

Typical gravel race bike geometry has become slacker over the past few years, adding stability in technical race segments and to assist riders when they become fatigued. Along with that, there’s also greater tyre clearance, with this typically having increased from the low 40s to 50mm or more.

The frame’s stack may still be lower than a gravel adventure bike though, allowing the rider to adopt a faster, more aero ride position.

Integration

Pretty much every performance bike now has cable integration, with brake hoses and, where there are any, gear cables fully enclosed through the handlebars and stem and into the head tube. It’s a trend in gravel race bikes too which, along with aero profiled bars, improves front-end aerodynamics.

Often integration means a one-piece bar and stem. It looks great and is more aero, but means any fit adjustment requires replacing the expensive bar/stem. It also precludes bar angle adjustment, so make sure you’re comfortable on your chosen component.

Aerodynamics

Integration is one factor in gravel race bike aerodynamics. As with road bikes, an aero frame profile is seen as a significant contributor of free speed in gravel races, so many gravel race bikes borrow aero tubes from their road bike brethren.

Winning times in gravel races are getting faster, although in general average speeds are still lower than in road races. That means that the best gravel race bikes are often aero tested at lower speeds than road bikes. A case in point is the latest Cannondale SuperX, which was aero tuned at 35km/h rather than the 45km/h Cannondale uses for its road race bikes. With the lower speeds, aero gains are lower but still significant.

Aerobars are also often used in gravel races to lower wind resistance, so the option to fit them is handy. Aero profiled bar/stems may prevent this or limit the options available, so you may need to replace them with a conventional round bar and separate stem. Canyon has got around this with the Grail by selling aero extensions specifically designed to fit the bike’s Pace cockpit.

Gearing

With the increasing speeds of gravel racing, the typical gravel bike gearing may be too low for some riders. Although complete bikes usually still come fitted with a gravel bike groupset, many gravel bikes are designed to allow riders to fit a road bike groupset. The Factor Elara, for example, will accept a 52t 1x chainring as well as a 2x groupset and many gravel race bikes can be fitted with chainrings larger than the subcompact cranksets typical for all-rounder and adventure gravel bikes.

If you want higher gearing for faster rides, many gravel race bikes can be bought frameset-only, so you can choose your own components and gear ratios.

Load carrying

Most gravel race bikes cut down on the mounting points of generalist gravel bikes and gravel adventure bikes. Nevertheless, gravel racers still need to eat, drink and carry spares, so you’ll still typically see a third bottle mounting point under the down tube and top tube bag bolts and often frame bag mounts. In-frame storage is often included.

Fork leg mounts and mudguard mounts are usually absent though, so don’t expect most gravel race bikes to be able to do double duty as a load carrier or all-weather road bike, although there are exceptions.

On-road use

If you read through our detailed reviews of the best gravel race bikes, you’ll find that many of them perform pretty well on road too, as you might expect from the features listed above. They come at a similar space from the opposite direction to the best all-road bikes, which ride well on road but perform pretty well on light gravel, although newer gravel race bikes are becoming increasingly specialised.

So if your riding is more road than gravel an all-road bike may be the way for you to go rather than a gravel race bike.
